title: Historical and Conditional Forecasts of Sampled Net-Position Peaks
subtitle: A retrospective benchmark on an FX record and Treasury position aggregates
abstract: We benchmark established forecasts of the 0.95 quantile of the largest absolute net position observed at issue and over the next H source records. Historical constructions are evaluated against ridge quantile regression (QR) and local quantiles using completed responses and matched-history controls. The FX evaluation archive had previously been inspected; the Treasury exercise replays a downloaded vintage by economic date rather than historical public release. On 6,625 FX origins, the declared six-record-horizon QR primary lowers mean pinball loss by 12.66% against its original rolling reference and 14.77% against a matched-history reference, with 376 breaches versus 332 and 360. On 277 weekly Treasury-aggregate origins, the separately fitted six-week QR primary raises loss by 50.79% and breaches from 28 to 54. Exploratory AR replay improves on matched increment translation in five of eight cells while breaches increase in all eight. Reweighting eight archived .95 reports distinguishes the FX short-horizon reductions in both mean error components from the small 24-record gain, which reverses above an underprediction/overprediction weight ratio of 20.63, near the stipulated 19. These retrospective comparisons establish source-, horizon-, history- and family-dependent rankings, without coverage guarantees or observed trading and funding benefits.

blocks.html: A terminal position forecast can miss a large intermediate magnitude that subsequently recedes. We study the largest absolute source-reported net position at issue and over the next H recorded observations. Its upper-quantile report provides a level against which subsequent recorded magnitudes can be monitored. Sampling and netting matter: the target does not reconstruct unobserved inter-record excursions, a complete hedged dealer book or a cash-funding requirement.

The empirical question is whether simple historical peak constructions remain competitive with established regression and local quantile methods fitted directly to this response. We compare historical headrooms (F), increment paths reanchored to the current signed position (S), and native historical peaks subject to the current magnitude floor (K). These historical rules already use the current magnitude or signed anchor. We use direct conditional methods as a shorthand for ridge quantile regression (QR), multivariate nearest-neighbor quantiles (KNN) and a scale-adjusted local variant. Earlier one-state retrieval remains a reference. The methods are evaluated on common issue origins, with controls matching completed-response histories and refit schedules.

The two declared primaries have opposite directions. At the six-record FX horizon, QR with 2,880 completed episodes lowers mean pinball loss by 12.66% against the original rolling 720-episode F rule and by 14.77% against matched-history F. Breaches increase to 376 from 332 and 360, respectively, while mean underprediction amount falls. The separately fitted six-week Treasury QR primary raises loss by 50.79% and increases breaches from 28 to 54 over 277 origins. All four Treasury QR cells lose to their own F controls. The weekly Treasury aggregate measures a different financial object from the individual-market-maker FX record; the two source primaries do not estimate a common replicated effect.

The contribution is a reproducible comparison on a common sampled-peak target. Direct regression and local quantiles can change the ranking of historical constructions even when completed-label histories and update schedules are matched. The favorable short-horizon FX comparison, adverse Treasury QR comparison and later AR results show that rankings depend on the measurement process, horizon, history and model family. Fixed-report loss decomposition further distinguishes reductions in both mean error components from a score gain near an asymmetric-weight crossing. The estimators and supporting finite geometry are established operations; the comparison does not identify the causal value of additional features.

Later exploratory additions retain the original primaries and every adverse comparison. AR(1) residual-block replay qualifies interpretations based on QR alone; rank, floor and horizon-order checks clarify the issued reports; linear weight sensitivity concerns eight archived .95 reports. These additions use previously inspected results. The FX evaluation archive had already been inspected before the conditional extension, and execution freezes do not restore an untouched holdout. The Treasury exercise uses a downloaded-vintage economic-date replay, rather than reconstructed historical public releases. Section 5 distinguishes the analysis stages and the supplement preserves their execution identities.

sections.title: 2. Closest work and established forecasting methods

blocks.html: Wisniewski, Lindsay and Lindsay (2020) already apply nearest-neighbor and other regression engines to this FX source family, using preceding positions and calendar or trading-session information. Their comparisons include quantile, conformal and normalized-conformal endpoint intervals. Chapter 6 of Wisniewski's thesis continues related regularized and normalized endpoint constructions (award year 2024; inspected cover 2023). Conditional regression, lag/calendar features, neighbors and normalization on these records are therefore precedents, rather than contributions of this study. Exact input-byte equality with the accepted version-2 member is not established.

Our response is a single upper quantile of an absolute multi-record maximum including the observed issue floor. A signed endpoint interval does not determine this peak: identical future-record marginals can yield different maxima when their dependence differs. The earlier paper averages two endpoint-quantile losses; its numbers cannot benchmark this single peak score. We instead refit a selected set of established engines to completed peak/headroom labels and evaluate the same response on common origins. This is not a reproduction of that earlier entire model suite.

Financial path extrema are established risk objects. MaxVaR studies the worst mark-to-market loss before a horizon under a portfolio-value first-passage framework (Boudoukh et al., 2004). Petrunia, Sabetti and Voia (2019, updated Discussion Paper 7) study the largest end-of-day net debit across ACSS participants, followed by block maxima or threshold excesses. Their cross-sectional terminal-debit maximum differs from a single series' future two-sided sampled peak. Van den Hoogen (2017) more directly defines an intraday liquidity buffer as a conditional quantile of the interval's maximum cumulative negative payment balance, using modeled transaction amounts and durations, simulated paths and EVT. Its directional cash-deficit target and confidential transaction inputs differ from this source-reported absolute position peak; that model is not reproduced here. These precedents rule out treating financial peak forecasting or a peak-to-quantile-buffer construction as new.

Prospective payment-system liquidity forecasting also has established precedents. Arjani, Li and Sabetti (2020) predict a remaining-day payment-demand/resource ratio and its threshold exceedance using payments and credit information. That ratio is a different functional from an absolute position peak or a directional timing peak. We neither reproduce their models nor observe the settlement inputs required to validate funding adequacy. The distinction further limits broad financial-target novelty claims.

Regression-quantile loss minimization is classical (Koenker and Bassett, 1978). Biau and Patra (2011) study sequential quantile prediction with lag-neighbor experts under stationarity, ergodicity and regularity assumptions. The fixed pools and delayed overlapping labels here do not inherit their consistency theorem. The comparison is deliberately bounded: quantile forests (Meinshausen, 2006), autoregressive quantiles such as CAViaR (Engle and Manganelli, 2004), sequential predictive conformal inference (Xu and Xie, 2023), and full volatility-updated or filtered historical simulation (Hull and White, 1998; Barone-Adesi et al., 1999) are established alternatives outside the executed menu.

Trajectory bands and financial horizon curves also predate this comparison. Conformalized Adaptive Forecasting of Heterogeneous Trajectories (Zhou, Lindemann and Sesia, 2024, arXiv v2) uses trajectory-level calibration and a cross-trajectory exchangeability premise. Sözen (2026) combines multi-horizon expected-shortfall forecasts, shape constraints and joint calibration. Their responses and assumptions differ from this position peak; an overlapping single archive is not automatically an exchangeable set of trajectories. Chronological slicing or response normalization alone transfers no simultaneous or conditional-coverage conclusion. We report realized loss, breaches and severity without borrowing those guarantees.

This study places selected mature methods on a common measured peak response, with a known floor, completed-label timing and construction/update controls. It provides a bounded empirical comparison rather than a new estimator. The directed literature search does not establish exhaustive priority for this exact target-and-data combination. The source evidence map records the consulted editions and selected reading ranges.

The FX input is the one-hour member of the Net Position Time Series Dataset, version 2: 18,576 records from 5 February 2014 01:00 through 24 January 2017 00:00. Wisniewski et al. (2020) describe aggregate client-flow positions across five liquid currency pairs for one market maker. We use datetime and the signed NetPosUsd scalar, rather than reconstructing raw currency positions, hedge transactions or cash movements. The source has 18,420 one-hour and 155 forty-nine-hour adjacent gaps. We preserve chronology without sorting, removing gap-crossing windows or interpolation. The timezone and historical publication/vintage convention remain unverified.

The Treasury source is New York Fed Primary Dealer Statistics series PDPOSGS-B, Treasury-bill long positions less short positions. FR 2004A supplies Wednesday-close positions at market/fair value. Its instructions use trade-date accounting, with specified buyback treatment on settlement date, and include eligible forward and when-issued outright positions; the series is not settled cash holdings (Board of Governors, March 2013 and July 2024 instructions). The accepted snapshot has 706 seven-day-spaced records from 3 April 2013 through 7 October 2026, in USD millions. It aggregates reporting dealers and can reflect valuation or reporting-composition changes. Taking an absolute value after summing signed positions permits cross-dealer cancellation: a small aggregate can coexist with large individual magnitudes (Duffie et al., 2023). It does not identify gross exposures or pure customer order flow.

This is a mean-filtered ordered-block historical comparison, not the full conditional-volatility filtered simulation of Hull and White (1998) or Barone-Adesi et al. (1999). It does not standardize/rescale residuals, fit GARCH, independently draw future steps or introduce Monte Carlo randomness. Conditional representativeness of historical residual blocks remains unverified; numerical OLS acceptance supplies no coverage or mean-reversion law. blocks.html: The analysis has distinct stages. The original construction study fixed its target-specific procedure before calculating its forecasts and losses. The subsequent one-state retrieval extension was conceived after those outcomes were inspected; Appendix B retains both complete menus. The conditional extension fixed its sources, features, menus, machine limits and comparison definitions before its new validation runs, then recorded every selected parameter before evaluation. Its FX evaluation archive had already been inspected. These execution freezes establish what ran, rather than an unseen evaluation or removal of earlier inspection.

AR replay, floor/horizon diagnostics, ordinary-rank sensitivity, late conditional-breach evidence and fixed-report weight sensitivity were added after earlier results were inspected. Each is explicitly exploratory and leaves the original primaries unchanged. The public supplements retain their complete menus, design/freezing chronology, input identities, numerical acceptance conditions, independent arithmetic checks and reproduction receipts. Archive verification, numerical reproduction and new financial validation are distinct: the first two do not supply an additional sample.

blocks.html: The H6 primary QR W2880 loss is USD 385,844.89, against USD 441,774.04 for original rolling F W720. The direct paired mean is −USD 55,929.15, or −12.660%. Against W2880 frozen F it is −14.767%; against frozen S at that same window it is also favorable. Thus the added conditional benchmark changes the older FX ranking. The cross-window primary changes history length and update frequency as well as the estimator; the matched-pool controls address part, but not all, of this procedural difference. Figure 1 places every selected conditional cell beside its same-history frozen F reference.

The H6 gain is not uniform risk improvement. QR has 376 strict breaches (5.675%) versus 332 (5.011%) for old rolling F. Mean underprediction amount falls from USD 166,531.06 to 156,123.03, while mean overprediction amount falls by USD 920,830.41. More occasions breach, with a lower unconditional underprediction contribution. Conditional severity uses the different method-specific event sets and cannot identify improvement on the same incidents. At W720, H6 QR improves on frozen F by only 2.117%, while scaled KNN is worse by 5.349%. Figure 2 separates the score, breach-frequency and mean-error changes for the fixed headline comparisons.

At H24, QR W2880 loss is USD 734,695.07 against USD 748,383.54 for old rolling S W720: −USD 13,688.47 (−1.829%). Breaches increase from 287 (4.332%) to 531 (8.015%); mean underprediction amount rises from USD 149,813.88 to 317,678.12, while overprediction amount falls. With W720, QR instead loses to frozen F by 31.504% and frozen S by 37.095%. Neither the broader model class nor a favorable short-horizon result provides a uniform advantage across history budgets.

The H6 primary loss difference is negative in both issue-year groups: −12.012% over 6,262 origins in 2016 and −29.513% over the 363-origin partial 2017. The latter contains 5.48% of all issue origins and contributes 8.64% of the H6 primary net gain and 6.87% of the matched-history H6 net gain. For both H6 comparisons, U and V fall in each issue-year group and on the fixed 947-origin grid. In contrast, H24 improves against its legacy reference by only 0.555% in 2016 and 33.007% in partial 2017; 70.83% of its small total net gain comes from that short tail segment, and U increases in both groups and on the 265-origin grid. Figure 3 shows the issue-year contrasts. The fixed H+1 grids retain favorable H6/H24 legacy-reference loss differences of −16.388%/−8.027%. These are decompositions and sensitivities of the same inspected record, not independent validation or a basis for retrospective forecast switching.

Its paired increase is 1,401.008 (+50.786%), with 54 rather than 28 strict breaches (19.495% versus 10.108%). Mean underprediction amount rises from 1,395.639 to 3,131.862 and overprediction amount falls from 28,656.166 to 23,688.088. Under the stipulated score, the reduced overprediction amount does not compensate for the more heavily weighted underprediction increase. This is an adverse accuracy result from numerically accepted fits, not a convergence failure.

Every Treasury QR cell loses to its own frozen F control: +83.354% and +50.786% at H6 for W52/W260, and +227.411% and +109.843% at H24. Short-history H24 QR breaches 132 of 277 responses. All four selected scaled-KNN cells also have higher loss than their matched F controls. The primary QR difference is adverse in each complete issue-year group from 2021 through 2025. Its favorable −14.404% in 2026 covers only 16 issue origins through April, with no breaches for either method. This partial period is retained, not used to rescue the primary.

Plain KNN W52 selects k=52 at both horizons and equals frozen F at every stored issue. The distance coordinates do not change membership in these rows; This is an ordinary validation-selected full-pool identity, rather than a response to fitting failure or evidence of a feature-membership gain. At W260, selected KNN has secondary all-origin loss reductions of 3.447% (H6) and 8.964% (H24) against F. These do not replace the QR primary, and no selected conditional procedure is descriptively below every retained historical reference at its horizon. Such a whole-menu observation is not a newly selected forecast rule.

The secondary H24 KNN W260 comparison has 13 versus 12 breaches and mean underprediction amount 327.816 versus 306.848, alongside reduced overprediction amount. On the single globally anchored 12-origin H+1 grid its mean loss is 3,111.788 against 2,807.400 for F, reversing to +10.842%. The H6 KNN sensitivity does not reverse: its 40-origin difference remains −22.071%. These exact grids remove shared recorded label observations but retain common training histories and possible time dependence. The sparse reversal does not identify a cause or prove an opposite population ranking; it does prevent a claim of a stable secondary ranking.

sections.title: 9. Loss-weight sensitivity of eight fixed reports

blocks.html: The main score fixes an underprediction/overprediction weight ratio of 19:1. We now vary that ratio for previously issued .95 reports. This changes the evaluation of fixed actions, rather than fitting other quantiles. For report m, U and V are its mean underprediction and overprediction amounts over the same origins. For 0<=a<=1 define:
J<sub>m</sub>(a)=a U<sub>m</sub>+(1-a)V<sub>m</sub>; r=a/(1-a); J<sub>m</sub>(.95)=L<sub>m,.95</sub>.

At a=0 or a=1 only one component remains; finite positive r corresponds to 0<a<1. For reports A and B the difference is a(U<sub>A</sub>−U<sub>B</sub>)+(1−a)(V<sub>A</sub>−V<sub>B</sub>). Reducing both components gives weak improvement for every constant nonnegative linear weighting, and strict improvement when a positively weighted component strictly decreases. Opposing component differences yield a crossing when it lies in the stated range. This elementary geometry establishes neither dominance under nonlinear or state-dependent costs nor dominance over every consistent .95 quantile score (Gneiting, 2011). A higher breach frequency remains possible when U falls.

blocks.html: The two FX H6 comparisons reduce both mean underprediction amount and mean overprediction amount. Their improvement therefore does not rely on the single 19:1 preference, even though strict breach occasions still increase. By contrast, the FX H24 legacy comparison increases U while reducing overprediction amount: its 1.829% pinball improvement reverses at r=20.630898 (a=0.953770), close to 19. The Treasury H6 primary becomes preferable only below r=2.861429 (a=0.741028); its adverse result at 19 remains intact. These are descriptive consequences of fixed sample means, not estimates of financing prices or risk preferences.

Within each source/H/W cell, the lower envelope is computed only over eight archived .95 reports: QR, KNN, scaled KNN, matched frozen F/S/K, AR and I. They share the completed-label history length and refit schedule, but this finite menu does not exhaust feasible reports. For example, C=B is feasible and has V=0, making it a minimizer at a=0 over all feasible reports; that floor-only action is absent from this eight-report menu. The reported endpoint winners therefore describe the menu, rather than all feasible decisions. Rolling and one-state reports are also excluded; the original cross-window primary references are separately labeled in Table 6. Appendix E retains all full and sparse-grid envelopes, endpoints and ties. Full-grid Treasury H6 W260 QR is never optimal among these eight reports, including both endpoints. At a=.95 the menu minimizer changes on four of eight sparse grids: FX H24 W720, Treasury H6 W52/W260 and Treasury H24 W52. Treasury H24 grids contain only 12 origins. These are dependent within-archive sensitivities, rather than four independent replication outcomes.

This analysis was conceived after earlier results and preliminary preference calculations were inspected. It reads saved aggregate means without accessing raw observations or refitting reports. The supplement preserves the before-run execution identities, both byte-identical result runs and the strengthened independent affine-inequality check. Rational calculations are exact for the saved decimal mean tokens, which summarize floating-point losses rather than infinite-precision raw observations. The resulting hindsight envelopes are descriptive objects, not deployment selectors.

The principal finding is variation in ranking. Long-history QR improves the six-record FX comparison and performs worse on the separately fitted Treasury aggregate. Exploratory AR replay improves on QR in all four Treasury cells and loses in three of four FX cells. Against matched S, AR improves mean loss in five cells and raises it in three, while breach occasions increase in all eight. Thus the adverse Treasury QR primary concerns the tested QR specifications, and the favorable AR cells do not establish a general advantage for conditional modeling.

Mean quantile loss and breach frequency answer different questions. The two H6 FX comparisons reduce U and V despite more strict breaches; their sample-average improvement persists under every constant nonnegative linear weighting of those components. Higher breach frequency rules out empirical first-order stochastic dominance in the favorable direction for the distribution of positive-part errors (P−C)<sub>+</sub>, including zeros: its empirical distribution function is lower at zero. A cost per breach or a nonlinear loss can therefore change the ranking. The smaller H24 FX legacy gain instead trades increased U for reduced V and reverses at ratio 20.63. These are properties of fixed reports under stipulated weights, rather than measured financing costs or uniformly improved tail risk.

The controls address only part of the procedural difference. F/K already use current magnitude and S uses the signed anchor; QR and local methods also change function class, regularization, local count, scaling, validation selection and raw lookback. Matching completed-response pools and refit schedules does not isolate a causal information effect. Each source is fitted and validated separately; fitted FX coefficients and transforms are not transferred to Treasury. The source primaries also differ in references, histories, update schedules, units and calendar horizons.

Limited validation budgets further restrict generalization. Five of eight QR selections lie at penalty-menu endpoints, including all four Treasury cells; this does not show that an untested penalty would help. The 52 consecutive Treasury validation origins contain at most three mutually observation-disjoint H24 label windows, without implying an effective sample size of three. Issue-year groups and sparse grids remain subdivisions of the inspected archives. They cannot replace compatible untouched financial records, and mature forecasting alternatives remain outside the tested menu.

Post-result diagnostics clarify the accepted reports without repairing them. The ordinary empirical-rank control retains the matched H6 QR improvement in FX and deterioration in Treasury. Separately fitted horizon reports can cross even though every realized target is ordered; numerical acceptance supplies no horizon-coherence guarantee. A binding floor is not an identified cause of the Treasury QR errors, and projection onto a known outcome floor differs from raising a long-horizon report to another learned report. Appendix D retains complete rank, floor and crossing results. Its late fixed-terminal conditional-breach calculations remain exploratory and provide no retrospective coverage certification for the selected analysis.

The remaining limits concern information, measurement and decisions. The Treasury economic-date replay does not reconstruct historical public releases or revisions, and its aggregate can conceal offsetting dealer positions. Both sources omit inter-record paths, book decomposition and the quotes, fills, hedges, cash flows, collateral and financing prices needed for an operational evaluation. Active inventory-sensitive quoting, as in Avellaneda and Stoikov (2008), changes the position process and is outside this passive exercise. Further compatible data, a defensible release clock and an observed decision link would answer stronger questions than another comparison on the same archives.

Established methods change the ranking of historical forecasts for the sampled net-position peak, with results depending on source, horizon, history and model family. The declared six-record FX QR primary lowers mean loss by 12.66%, with a 14.77% matched-history reduction and more breach occasions. The separately fitted six-week Treasury QR primary raises loss by 50.79% and increases breaches. Later AR replay improves on QR in every Treasury cell while increasing breaches relative to matched increment translation in all eight cells. Fixed-report weight sensitivity separates the short-horizon FX reductions in both mean error components from the near-threshold long-horizon gain; sparse-grid reversals further limit claims of stable rankings. The retained evidence supports a bounded retrospective benchmark using mature methods. It establishes neither a new estimator, conditional coverage nor an observed benefit from changing trading, funding or risk-limit decisions.

Both A<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>i</sub> are at least B. The projection C<sub>B</sub> is nondecreasing and 1-Lipschitz. It commutes with a finite order statistic, as does a common translation. Among all size-m subsets, selecting the m smallest signed distances minimizes the largest selected distance: any alternative must include an element at least as far away as the mth ordered distance. This finite minimax fact, with the declared tie convention, concerns the signed radius. blocks.html: For interpretation, fix arbitrary coefficients c and phi and define residuals epsilon(s)=N(s+1)−c−phi N(s). Replay a historical window's ordered residuals from query x. The coefficients are fixed after a refit; this algebra does not assert a true dynamic law or a martingale-difference property. Denote replay by M and raw translation by W. Subtracting the recursions and using induction gives
M<sub>i,h</sub>(x)=N<sub>i+h</sub>+φ<super>h</super>(x−N<sub>i</sub>);   W<sub>i,h</sub>(x)=N<sub>i+h</sub>+(x−N<sub>i</sub>).
Taking the maximum absolute path value yields
|max<sub>h</sub>|W<sub>i,h</sub>(x)|−max<sub>h</sub>|M<sub>i,h</sub>(x)||≤max<sub>0≤h≤H</sub>|1−φ<super>h</super>| |x−N<sub>i</sub>|.

For 0≤φ≤1 the coefficient is 1−φ<super>H</super>; at φ=1 the paths coincide. The identity needs no residual law, while treating past residuals as representative of future conditional residuals is a separate assumption. Section 8 fits a specified mean recursion and compares realized loss, but does not validate that conditional residual-representativeness assumption. The extrema suffice to evaluate the peak after raw translation, but generally not after the dynamic correction, which depends on path order. The same-rank reports inherit a deterministic bound with max over historical anchor distances, not a guaranteed sign of loss improvement. Conditional validity remains a separate question.

An objective-gap bound does not bound issued-report differences or ranking sensitivity: with an unpenalized intercept the pinball objective can be flat or nearly flat. For example, at real tau=19/20, an intercept-only sample of nineteen zeros and one M>0 has every intercept in [0,M] as a minimizer. A later exploratory diagnostic uses the bounded strict hit I=1{P>C}, with equality a nonbreach, and the null that its conditional expectation given full issue information is at most alpha=1/20 at every declared issue. It is not unconditional equal-loss testing or exact exceedance identification at a floor atom. Conditional-moment betting and delayed binary evidence are mature precedents (Casgrain et al., 2023, v2; Henzi and Ziegel, 2022, v3). For a fixed alternative u in [alpha,1], the hit/no-hit factor is u/alpha or (1−u)/(1−alpha); its null conditional expectation is at most one. Every globally anchored H+1 phase retains only issues whose previous same-phase target has resolved.
E<sub>n,k</sub> = [1/(1−α)] ∫<sub>α</sub><super>1</super> (u/α)<super>k</super> [(1−u)/(1−α)]<super>n−k</super> du.
E<sub>cell</sub> = [1/(H+1)] ∑<sub>r=0</sub><super>H</super> E<sub>n(r),k(r)</sub>; α=1/20.

The prior mixes each whole phase product, then all phases receive equal weight; empty phases have value one. Iterated expectation and nonnegative averaging justify a fixed-terminal e-value for a genuinely fixed causal procedure under the stated null, without independence, stationarity or a financial-magnitude moment assumption. This gives no full-filtration supermartingale or arbitrary-stopping claim. The complete matched family has 56 labels, including aliases, and excludes 24 rolling and 18 one-state reports. Its formal reference threshold is 56/(1/20)=1120. Because this diagnostic and family were chosen after inspecting results, the crossings do not obtain retrospective empirical five-percent familywise error control. The fixed-procedure proof also does not establish individually calibrated e-values or p-values for this same-sample, post-selected analysis: selection need not be measurable at the original issue times. No prior, phase or menu was retuned.

After inspecting both source archives and the previous results, we fixed one further eight-cell supplement and published a 16-file execution freeze before its financial calculation. At each original evaluation-segment refit, the added intercept-only report uses the same W completed headrooms and original update schedule as frozen F. Dividing all headrooms by a positive training-response scale and multiplying the fitted intercept back by that scale preserves the rank and the minimizer interval in native units.
